subtopic: Managing time in a heavy semester
subtype: Approach: prioritising urgent versus important tasks [Thinking]
passage:
Subject: Stepping back from the poster job

Dear Seema,

I owe you an honest note. This week I have two graded assignments, the lab file and the club fest, all before Saturday. Last night I wrote them in a row with the date and the marks beside each. The assignments count for marks and cannot move. The lab file is due Thursday morning and is worth the most. The fest posters are not due till next week, and I realise someone else can do them. If I keep all four, all four will be done badly. So I have to let the posters go.

I am sorry to drop this at short notice. I will pass on my sketches tonight and help with hanging them if I can.

Deepika

qa.q: Which day is the lab file due?
qa.a: The lab file is due Thursday morning.

qa.q: What did Deepika think when writing the tasks in a row with dates and marks?
qa.a: Deepika felt uneasy and a little guilty, realising that all four tasks could not be done well, so the least valuable one, the posters, had to be dropped.

qa.q: What other approach could Deepika try before dropping the posters, and why?
qa.a: Deepika could ask Seema to split the poster work in two, since sharing the job might keep it alive without hurting the marks.

qa.q: How might Seema see the note arriving at short notice?
qa.a: Seema may feel worried about finding a new helper, but honest words and a promise of the sketches make it easier to plan around.

grounding: A student facing heavy deadlines sorts tasks by due date and marks and drops the least valuable item.
